Some programs (that you might not think should download) can request upgrade download in background.

Can you provide your processes as well? The context, given the screenshot is not adequate enough to deduce anything.

It's probably the Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) downloading updates for the Windows Update Service. It is supposed to be a lightweight transfer agent that runs when network traffic is low and pauses when demand increases. BITS often runs transfers over a long time because the transfer rate is low and Windows Update patches can be hundreds of MB or larger if many are available. You might want to see if your Windows Update Service is set to automatically download updates. You can set it to manual updates then restart to see if the behavior stops. Hope this helps.

EDIT: If you don't already have it, I recommend downloading Process Explorer (Microsoft) to see which processes are using network bandwidth. It will also help you determine which SVCHOST.exe process BITS is living in to determine if it is truly the culprit.

For me it's not about genres, it's about gameplay characteristics. The things I like the most are:

  • Well thought controls that let you move the character as naturally as possible but with enough complexity that the player can develop skill. It's not about the number of controls, a good game can have smooth, sophisticated controls even if you can only run or jump, such as in Mario. I loved the controls in Shadow of the Colossus.

  • Procedural content, so that the game can extend its lifetime almost indefinitely, as long as it doesn't repeat itself too much. Of course Dwarf Fortress wins hands down here, but everything goes as long as I feel something was not designed by someone but emerged "spontaneously". Most games just end up being repetitive, uninspiring or too much random, it's still something needing more years of evolution in technology and design principles IMO. On a side note, I bought Minecraft because of that but it definitely fails giving unique, emergent experiences even if it's all about it, so I have no good examples to give.

  • Freedom of choice, including but not limited to free-roaming, sandbox or character customization. Not a fan of customizability of the game itself, I'd rather have a well designed, robust gameplay from experienced devs than having to design it by myself with options, mods and so on. All I ask for is choice and freedom. Of course Elder Scrolls and GTA series are know for that but it's mostly fluff IMO because you always end up doing the same things the devs designed for you (go there, kill those, take that...). Still waiting for a good title with such premises.

  • Immersion and suspension of disbelief. It's not about graphics or strict realism, it's about a world where you're not constantly met with inconsistent mechanics and too much meta-game semantics but you're instead sucked in, so to speak, so I'm quite a fan of a reasonable level of simulation, good AI, transparent interface and staying away from logical loopholes in stories. It doesn't have to be a modern game, even the first Silent Hills does a great job even if it falls flat here and there with its silly puzzles.

  • Innovation. I spent 35 years gaming so don't spoonfeed me the same old crap. New ideas, experimentation, anything that makes a genre make even a small step further is a must. It doesn't have to be a genre-redefining game such as Half Life 2 or Minecraft, all I ask for is progression, evolution; for example, Halo did a very good job at innovating FPSs even if it didn't add a whole new paradigm.

Hard question. I'd have to say well-designed, player-centric games. When a developer puts time into planning, testing, and fine-tuning a game I can feel the difference. It's why I can spend hours playing Binding of Isaac (essentially a flash game), but can barely stand some of the free to wait games coming out of the triple AAA's lately.
